Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.item: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'the people responsible have faced no consequences' is hard to reconcile unless there was a clear perpetrator such as major medical negligence. Nothing else in the profile suggests an interpersonal or negligence-based trauma, so this appraisal appears mismatched to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
issues.explanation: A specific perfume or cologne as a trigger is not impossible, but in the context of life-threatening illness it usually needs some link to a person or setting. Here, the rest of the profile does not support an interpersonal perpetrator or a distinctive sensory cue tied to treatment, making this trigger weakly grounded and less coherent with the other selected items.

vignette:
Marina had been a 39-year-old dentist when the illness struck, someone used to being composed in a clinic, in control of sharp instruments and frightened patients alike. The first shock came not in a dramatic collapse but in the slow certainty that something was seriously wrong: breathlessness that did not settle, weakness that made ordinary movement feel unsafe, and then the hospital admission where the antiseptic smell seemed to announce danger before anyone spoke. In the ward, with monitors beeping and decisions happening around her, what distressed her most was the feeling of having no options. She had been confined to bed, dependent on others for basic care, and she later described that period as the moment she realised her body could not be trusted. When she thinks back to that time now, old photos from before the illness can catch her unexpectedly and pull her straight into the belief that she has permanently changed for the worse, as if the healthy woman in those pictures belonged to someone else. The smell of a hospital corridor or disinfectant in a dental clinic can have the same effect: it does not merely remind her of the past, it makes her feel weak again, as though the illness is still waiting just beneath the surface.

After discharge, Marina tried to return to work, but the meaning she had taken from the illness travelled with her into everyday life. She became watchful of any sensation in her own body, checking for fatigue, shortness of breath, or any sign that she was slipping back into danger. That vigilance only confirmed her fear that she could no longer trust her own body, and from there the conclusion felt personal and harsh: she was weak, permanently altered, less reliable than she had once been. The more she noticed these thoughts, the more she pulled back from people. She stopped talking openly about the illness or what it had been like in hospital, even with her partner, because putting it into words made it feel immediate and humiliating; she feared being seen as fragile. She also began avoiding paying attention to or looking at her own body, skipping mirrors when she could and brushing off any physical concern rather than examining it closely. In the clinic she could function for short periods, but the smell of antiseptic or the sense of being cornered in a packed schedule could make her feel trapped with no easy exit, and the fear of that sensation made her keep conversations brief and keep people at a distance. The less she spoke and the more she withdrew, the more her own account of the illness narrowed around weakness and damage, until the avoidance itself seemed to confirm that she had become someone permanently altered who could not cope the way she once had.

Over time, the strategy of keeping everything contained made the illness loom larger in her mind. Because she rarely talked about it, there was little chance to test whether others saw her as broken, and in the silence she returned again and again to the thought that she was weak and that her body was unreliable. That conviction made each trigger more potent: old photos felt like proof of what she had lost, the smell of hospital disinfectant carried her back to the helplessness of lying there with no options, and even busy moments at work could turn threatening if she felt physically trapped or unable to leave. The pattern narrowed her life in practical ways. She began turning down dinners, avoiding friends who might ask how she had really been, and keeping emotional distance from her partner when he tried to discuss the illness or its aftermath. At work, she remained competent, but she found excuses to step away from patients if her body sensations became too noticeable, anxious that any lapse would expose her weakness. By the time she sought help, her distress had become hard to dismiss. She was tired of organising her life around avoiding her own body, avoiding other people, and avoiding any conversation that might stir up what happened. What finally brought Marina in was the fear that the illness had not only scared her, but had rewritten who she was, and she wanted to know whether she could ever trust her body again without feeling that she had to live as if she were already broken.
